claim: At the Drosophila melanogaster larval neuromuscular junction (NMJ), a homeostatic system detects impaired postsynaptic sensitivity to neurotransmitter and activates a retrograde signal that restores synaptic function by adjusting neurotransmitter release.
source: At the NMJ, a homeostatic system detects impaired postsynaptic sensitivity to neurotransmitter and activates a retrograde signal that restores synaptic function by adjusting neurotransmitter release.
evidence: This is a general statement about the homeostatic plasticity mechanism at the NMJ, supported by the broader literature and the experimental context of the study.

claim: Homeostatic plasticity at the NMJ has been separated into temporally distinct phases: induction and maintenance.
source: This process has been separated into temporally distinct phases, induction and maintenance.
evidence: This statement describes the conceptual framework used in the field and in this study.

claim: A signaling system consisting of PLCβ, inositol triphosphate (IP3), IP3 receptors, and Ryanodine receptors is required only for the maintenance of homeostatic plasticity.
source: Combining genetics, pharmacology, and electrophysiology, we find that a signaling system consisting of PLCβ, inositol triphosphate (IP3), IP3 receptors, and Ryanodine receptors is required only for the maintenance of homeostatic plasticity.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by multiple genetic and pharmacological experiments presented in the manuscript.

claim: The NMJ is capable of inducing homeostatic signaling even when its sustained maintenance process is absent.
source: We also find that the NMJ is capable of inducing homeostatic signaling even when its sustained maintenance process is absent.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experiments showing PHP induction in conditions where maintenance is blocked.

claim: Concurrent knockdown of GluRIII and Plc21C gene functions by RNAi leaves homeostatic potentiation only partly intact.
source: By contrast, concurrent knockdown of GluRIII and Plc21C gene functions by RNAi (Pre-+Post Gal4>>UAS-GluRIII[RNAi]+Plc21C[RNAi]) leaves this form of homeostatic potentiation only partly intact (Figure 1A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data presented in Figure 1.

claim: Partial loss of Plc21C gene function is not sufficient to block the rapid induction of PHP.
source: Thus, partial loss of Plc21C gene function is not a sufficient condition to block the rapid induction of PHP.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from experiments showing that PhTox-induced PHP occurs normally in Plc21C knockdown backgrounds (Figure 1E-H).

claim: A rapid induction of PHP is possible at a synapse already undergoing a sustained maintenance of PHP.
source: This result indicated that a rapid induction of PHP was possible at a synapse already undergoing a sustained maintenance of PHP.
evidence: This is supported by experiments applying PhTox to UAS-GluRIII[RNAi] synapses (Figure 1I-L).

claim: Acute PHP induction does not require intact PHP maintenance and PLCβ plays a maintenance role.
source: Collectively, these data suggest that acute PHP induction does not require intact PHP maintenance and that PLCβ plays a maintenance role.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from experiments showing PHP induction in conditions where maintenance is impaired by Plc21C knockdown.

claim: Concomitant pre-and postsynaptic expression of UAS-IP3-sponge transgenes completely blocked the long-term expression of PHP.
source: Concomitant pre-and postsynaptic expression of UAS-IP3-sponge transgenes completely blocked the long-term expression of PHP (Figure 2B–E).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data in Figure 2.

claim: UAS-IP3-sponge expression alone does not block the rapid induction of PHP.
source: Following PhTox treatment, synapses expressing UAS-IP3-sponge in pre- and postsynaptic tissues showed a significant decrease in mEPSP amplitude compared to non-PhTox controls (Figure 2F), and yet they had steady EPSP amplitudes (Figure 2G) because of a robust increase in QC (Figure 2H). This result indicated that UAS-IP3-sponge expression left the rapid induction mechanisms of PHP intact.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data showing successful PHP induction despite IP3 sequestration (Figure 2F-H).

claim: The rapid induction of PHP is possible for third instar larval NMJs that had blocked PHP maintenance throughout life.
source: We next tested if the rapid induction of PHP was possible for third instar larval NMJs that had blocked PHP maintenance throughout life. To do this, we applied PhTox to NMJs expressing UAS-IP3-sponge in a UAS-GluRIII[RNAi] background. Even in this genetic background, we found that the rapid induction of PHP remained intact following PhTox treatment (Figure 2F–H).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data showing PHP induction in a double-challenged condition (Figure 2F-H).

claim: Chronic expression of the UAS-IP3-sponge transgene does not cause aberrant NMJ development or synapse undergrowth.
source: We observed no significant differences versus control in bouton number for any condition, for either segment A2 or A3 – including the genetic background where we co-expressed UAS-IP3-sponge and UAS-GluRIII[RNAi] (Figure 3F). There were also no significant differences versus control in bouton number normalized per unit muscle area (Figure 3G) (Figure 3—source data 1 for raw bouton count and muscle size data). These data indicate that when IP3 is sequestered, synapse undergrowth is not causal for a PHP block.
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining and bouton counting data (Figure 3).

claim: Acute application of 20 μM Xestospongin C to GluRIIASP16 null mutant NMJs blocks the long-term maintenance of PHP.
source: GluRIIASP16 NMJ preparations acutely treated with 20 μM Xestospongin C (10 min) displayed an expected decrease in mEPSP amplitude compared to non-GluRIIASP16 controls (Figure 4A). However, these drug-treated NMJs failed to show an increase in QC (Figure 4C). This resulted in markedly decreased evoked amplitudes (Figure 4B,G). Thus, not only did 20 μM Xestospongin C induce a block of PHP maintenance, but it was capable of extinguishing this long-term maintenance process on a timescale of minutes.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data showing loss of PHP with Xestospongin C treatment (Figure 4).

claim: 20 μM Xestospongin C does not impair baseline neurotransmission in a wild-type background.
source: Importantly, 20 μM Xestospongin C did not impair baseline neurotransmission in a wild-type background (Figure 4B,G); this suggests that 20 μM Xestospongin C does not impair the function of other important voltage-gated channels at the Drosophila NMJ.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data showing normal baseline transmission with drug treatment (Figure 4).

claim: Acute application of 20 μM Xestospongin C does not block the rapid induction of PHP.
source: Next, we tested if acute application of 20 μM Xestospongin C could block the rapid induction of PHP. We applied 20 μM Xestospongin C to wild-type NMJs concurrently with 20 μM PhTox. Quantal size was markedly diminished compared to the non-PhTox control (Figure 4D; vehicle control dataset same as in 4A-C). Yet evoked amplitudes remained near control levels (Figure 4E,G) because the rapid induction of PHP was intact (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data showing successful PHP induction with concurrent Xestospongin C and PhTox treatment (Figure 4D-F).

claim: Acute application of both 1 μM and 10 μM 2-APB to GluRIIASP16 null NMJs blocks the maintenance of PHP.
source: We applied both 1 μM and 10 μM 2-APB to GluRIIASP16 null NMJs. Both drug concentrations resulted in a failure to increase QC compared to drug-treated wild-type controls; this resulted in small evoked events for the drug-treated GluRIIASP16 NMJs because PHP maintenance was blocked (Figure 5A–C,G) (Supplementary file 4 for summary Figure 5 data) (Figure 5—source data 1 for raw data).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data showing loss of PHP with 2-APB treatment (Figure 5).

claim: 1 μM 2-APB does not block the PhTox-induced rapid induction of PHP.
source: Next, we tested if 2-APB blocks the PhTox-induced rapid induction of PHP. We applied 1 μM 2-APB concurrently with 20 μM PhTox. Evoked potentials remained near the level of 2-APB-treated NMJs without PhTox (Figure 5E,H) because 1 μM 2-APB left the rapid induction of PHP intact (Figure 5D–F).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data showing successful PHP induction with concurrent 2-APB and PhTox treatment (Figure 5D-F).

claim: 2-APB potentiated baseline neurotransmission in a dose-dependent manner.
source: We note that 2-APB potentiated baseline neurotransmission, seemingly in a dose-dependent way (Figure 5B,G). This potentiation likely means that 2-APB had off-target effects at the NMJ in addition to IP3Rs.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data showing increased EPSP amplitudes with 2-APB treatment (Figure 5B,G).

claim: Acute application of either 100 μM Ryanodine or 10 μM Dantrolene to GluRIIA null preparations results in failure of PHP maintenance.
source: Acute application of either 100 μM Ryanodine or 10 μM Dantrolene to GluRIIA null preparations resulted in failure of PHP maintenance. QC did not increase for the homeostatically challenged condition (GluRIIA +drug) versus the unchallenged condition (wild-type +drug) (Figure 6A–C) (Supplementary file 5 for summary Figure 6 data) (Figure 6—source data 1 for raw data).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data showing loss of PHP with RyR inhibitor treatment (Figure 6).

claim: Acute application of 10 μM Dantrolene does not disrupt the short-term induction of PHP.
source: Next, we tested whether RyR inhibition could block the rapid induction of PHP. As was the case with IP3R inhibition, acute application of 10 μM Dantrolene to PhTox-treated NMJs did not disrupt the short-term induction of PHP (Figure 6D–F).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data showing successful PHP induction with Dantrolene treatment (Figure 6D-F).

claim: In the GluRIII[RNAi] genetic background with dual Dantrolene application and UAS-IP3-sponge expression, the PHP impairment is indistinguishable from the impairment elicited by Dantrolene alone or UAS-IP3-sponge alone.
source: When we combined Dantrolene application and UAS-IP3-sponge expression in the GluRIII[RNAi] background, the PHP impairment was indistinguishable from the impairment elicited by Dantrolene alone or UAS-IP3-sponge alone (Figure 7A–D) (Supplementary file 6 for summary Figure 7 data) (Figure 7—source data 1 for raw data).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data showing non-additive effects of dual manipulation (Figure 7).

claim: IP3 sequestration and RyR blockade disrupt the long-term maintenance of PHP as part of a shared process, either via a single linear pathway or convergent pathways.
source: The data are consistent with a model in which IP3 sequestration and RyR blockade disrupt the long-term maintenance of PHP as part of a shared process, either via a single linear pathway or convergent pathways.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the non-additive effects observed in the dual manipulation experiments.

claim: Chronic Plc21C gene knockdown in the muscle alone is not sufficient to impair PHP.
source: Our prior work showed that chronic Plc21C gene knockdown in the muscle alone is not sufficient to impair PHP (Brusich et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a reference to prior published work by the authors.

claim: Expression of UAS-IP3-sponge in either neuron or muscle alone does not fully block PHP maintenance.
source: Surprisingly, we did not localize the full block of PHP maintenance to a single tissue. For expression in either tissue alone, there was still a small increase in QC in a Gal4 >>UAS-IP3-sponge + GluRIIASPSP16 genetic condition, compared to control Gal4 >>UAS-IP3-sponge expression in an unchallenged background (Figure 8C,F).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data showing partial PHP with single-tissue IP3 sequestration (Figure 8).

claim: The maintenance of PHP can be fully erased by IP3 sequestration only if this is done in a dual tissue manner.
source: Combined with our prior data (Figure 2), we conclude that the maintenance of PHP can be fully erased by IP3 sequestration – but only if this is done in a dual tissue manner.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from comparing dual-tissue and single-tissue IP3 sequestration effects.

claim: Sequestration of cellular IP3 at the NMJ does not directly alter the Ca2+-dependence of synaptic release at the presynaptic NMJ.
source: The Ca2+ cooperativity of release was steady between the three conditions (Figure 8H,I), indicating that sequestration of cellular IP3 at the NMJ does not directly alter the Ca2+-dependence of synaptic release at the presynaptic NMJ.
evidence: This is supported by calcium cooperativity measurements (Figure 8H,I).

claim: The short-term induction and long-term maintenance of PHP are separable by genetic and pharmacological manipulations.
source: Our data support two core findings. The first is that the short-term induction and long-term maintenance of PHP are separable by genetic and pharmacological manipulations.
evidence: This is a summary of the primary findings of the study.

claim: An IP3-mediated signaling system is specifically required for the maintenance of PHP.
source: The second is that an IP3-mediated signaling system is specifically required for the maintenance of PHP (Figure 9).
evidence: This is a summary of the primary findings of the study.

claim: Synaptic scaling was initially shown to be a slow, chronically executed process.
source: Synaptic scaling was initially shown to be a slow, chronically executed process (O'Brien et al., 1998; Turrigiano et al., 1998), but it is also possible for faster scaling mechanisms to be mobilized if multiple synaptic sites are concurrently inhibited (Sutton et al., 2006).
evidence: This statement references prior published work on synaptic scaling.

claim: For the NMJ, homeostatic signaling is triggered by short-term challenges to synapse function.
source: For the NMJ, homeostatic signaling is triggered by short-term challenges to synapse function (Frank et al., 2006; Wang et al., 2016b), but it is also maintained for extended developmental time in the face of chronic challenges (Cull-Candy et al., 1980; Davis et al., 1998; DiAntonio et al., 1999; Petersen et al., 1997; Plomp et al., 1992).
evidence: This statement references prior published work on NMJ homeostatic plasticity.

claim: At the Drosophila NMJ, reduced sensitivity to single vesicles of glutamate initiates a retrograde, muscle-to-nerve signaling cascade that induces increased neurotransmitter vesicle release.
source: At this NMJ, reduced sensitivity to single vesicles of glutamate initiates a retrograde, muscle-to-nerve signaling cascade that induces increased neurotransmitter vesicle release, or quantal content (QC). As a result, the NMJ maintains a normal postsynaptic response level (Frank et al., 2006; Petersen et al., 1997).
evidence: This statement describes the basic mechanism of PHP at the NMJ, referencing prior work.

claim: The increase in quantal content during PHP depends upon the successful execution of discrete presynaptic events, such as increases in neuronal Ca2+ influx and an increase in the size of the readily releasable pool (RRP) of synaptic vesicles.
source: Mechanistically, this increase in QC depends upon the successful execution of discrete presynaptic events, such as increases in neuronal Ca2+ influx and an increase in the size of the readily releasable pool (RRP) of synaptic vesicles (Frank et al., 2006; Müller and Davis, 2012; Müller et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement describes the presynaptic mechanisms underlying PHP, referencing prior work.

claim: Acute pharmacological inhibition of postsynaptic glutamate receptors initiates a rapid induction of PHP that restores synaptic output in minutes.
source: Acute pharmacological inhibition of postsynaptic glutamate receptors initiates a rapid induction of PHP that restores synaptic output in minutes (Frank et al., 2006).
evidence: This statement describes the acute induction of PHP, referencing prior work.

claim: Genetic lesions and other long-term reductions of NMJ sensitivity to neurotransmitter induce PHP in a way that is sustained throughout life.
source: By contrast, genetic lesions and other long-term reductions of NMJ sensitivity to neurotransmitter induce PHP in a way that is sustained throughout life (Brusich et al., 2015; Davis et al., 1998; DiAntonio et al., 1999; Paradis et al., 2001; Petersen et al., 1997).
evidence: This statement describes the chronic maintenance of PHP, referencing prior work.

claim: Plc21C encodes a Drosophila Phospholipase Cβ (PLCβ) homolog known to be neuronally expressed.
source: Plc21C encodes a Drosophila Phospholipase Cβ (PLCβ) homolog known to be neuronally expressed (Shortridge et al., 1991) – but recent ribosomal profiling data also indicates possible muscle expression of Plc21C (Chen and Dickman, 2017).
evidence: This statement describes the expression pattern of Plc21C, referencing prior work.

claim: Once PLCβ is activated by Gαq, it cleaves the membrane lipid phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate (PIP2) into diacylglycerol (DAG) and inositol triphosphate (IP3).
source: In canonical signaling pathways, once PLCβ is activated by Gαq, it cleaves the membrane lipid phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate (PIP2) into diacylglycerol (DAG) and inositol triphosphate (IP3).
evidence: This statement describes the canonical function of PLCβ, drawing on established knowledge.

claim: DAG can affect synaptic function by activating Protein Kinase C (PKC), while IP3 binds its receptor (IP3R) to trigger release of calcium from intracellular stores.
source: DAG can affect synaptic function by activating Protein Kinase C (PKC), while IP3 binds its receptor (IP3R) to trigger release of calcium from intracellular stores (Kadamur and Ross, 2013; Philip et al., 2010; Tedford and Zamponi, 2006).
evidence: This statement describes the downstream effects of PLCβ signaling, referencing prior work.

claim: Neither PLCβ, nor IP3R, nor RyR are required for the rapid induction of PHP.
source: We found that neither PLCβ, nor IP3R, nor RyR are required for the rapid induction of PHP.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by multiple experiments.

claim: NMJs are capable of rapidly inducing PHP even when the sustained expression of PHP is already blocked by impairments in PLCβ, IP3R, or RyR signaling.
source: Surprisingly, we found that NMJs are capable of rapidly inducing PHP – even when the sustained expression of PHP is already blocked by impairments in PLCβ, IP3R, or RyR signaling.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by multiple experiments.

claim: Even though there is compelling evidence that parts of the induction and maintenance signaling mechanisms overlap, it is also true that acute PHP is possible in scenarios where long-term PHP is not.
source: Even though there is compelling evidence that parts of the induction and maintenance signaling mechanisms overlap (Goel et al., 2017), it is also true that acute PHP is possible in scenarios where long-term PHP is not.
evidence: This is a summary statement reconciling the findings with prior work.

claim: Pre-+Post Gal4>>UAS-GluRIII[RNAi] NMJs have decreased quantal size (mEPSP) and an offsetting, homeostatic increase in quantal content (QC).
source: Pre-+Post Gal4>>UAS-GluRIII[RNAi] NMJs have decreased quantal size (mEPSP, Figure 1A) and an offsetting, homeostatic increase in quantal content (QC, Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data presented in Figure 1.

claim: The homeostatic increase in quantal content in Pre-+Post Gal4>>UAS-GluRIII[RNAi] NMJs keeps excitatory postsynaptic potentials (EPSPs) at control levels.
source: This increase in release keeps excitatory postsynaptic potentials (EPSPs) at control levels (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data presented in Figure 1.

claim: Xestospongin C is a membrane-permeable drug that disrupts intracellular calcium release directly via non-competitive inhibition of IP3Rs.
source: Xestospongin C is a membrane-permeable drug that disrupts intracellular calcium release directly via non-competitive inhibition of IP3Rs (Gafni et al., 1997; Wilcox et al., 1998).
evidence: This statement describes the known mechanism of Xestospongin C, referencing prior work.

claim: Xestospongin C has been previously shown to inhibit Drosophila IP3Rs.
source: Xestospongin C has been previously shown to inhibit Drosophila IP3Rs (Vázquez-Martínez et al., 2003).
evidence: This statement references prior work demonstrating the effect of Xestospongin C on Drosophila IP3Rs.

claim: Xestospongin C may act indirectly by inhibiting SERCA, which could lead to depletion of intracellular calcium stores.
source: There are caveats to its use; Xestospongin C may act indirectly by inhibiting SERCA, which could lead to depletion of intracellular calcium stores (Castonguay and Robitaille, 2002).
evidence: This statement describes a potential off-target effect of Xestospongin C, referencing prior work.

claim: Xestospongin C has been demonstrated to impair voltage-gated Ca2+ and K+ currents in guinea pig smooth muscle.
source: Moreover, Xestospongin C has been demonstrated to impair voltage-gated Ca2+ and K+ currents in guinea pig smooth muscle (Ozaki et al., 2002).
evidence: This statement describes a potential off-target effect of Xestospongin C, referencing prior work.

claim: 2-APB is a membrane-permeable drug that is known to impair IP3R.
source: 2-APB is a membrane-permeable drug that has variable effects. It is known to impair IP3R (Diver et al., 2001; Maruyama et al., 1997).
evidence: This statement describes the known mechanism of 2-APB, referencing prior work.

claim: 2-APB can impair targets such as Transient Receptor Potential (TRP) channels.
source: There are also reports that 2-APB can impair targets such as Transient Receptor Potential (TRP) channels (Bootman et al., 2002; Xu et al., 2005).
evidence: This statement describes a potential off-target effect of 2-APB, referencing prior work.

claim: Ryanodine receptors (RyRs) mediate release of calcium from ER stores.
source: Ryanodine receptors (RyRs) also mediate release of calcium from ER stores (Berridge, 1998; Simkus and Stricker, 2002).
evidence: This statement describes the known function of RyRs, referencing prior work.

claim: RyRs are localized to the ER in excitable tissues like neurons and muscle.
source: RyRs are localized to the ER in excitable tissues like neurons and muscle (Santulli and Marks, 2015; Santulli et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement describes the localization of RyRs, referencing prior work.

claim: In some tissues, RyR is activated by IP3R-mediated Ca2+ release, in a signaling process termed Calcium-Induced Calcium Release (CICR).
source: In some tissues, RyR is activated by IP3R-mediated Ca2+ release, in a signaling process termed Calcium-Induced Calcium Release (CICR) (Berridge, 1998).
evidence: This statement describes a known signaling mechanism involving RyR and IP3R, referencing prior work.

claim: IP3Rs and RyRs have been placed together in CICR signaling processes in other systems.
source: IP3Rs and RyRs have been placed together in CICR signaling processes in other systems, and our group has also identified overlapping functions of IP3R and RyR at the NMJ (Brusich et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement references prior work on CICR and the authors' own prior work.

claim: ER is known to localize throughout neurons in Drosophila, including synaptic terminals.
source: ER is known to localize throughout neurons in Drosophila, including synaptic terminals (Summerville et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement describes the localization of ER in Drosophila neurons, referencing prior work.

claim: Recent studies have implicated ER resident proteins in the execution of PHP at the Drosophila NMJ.
source: Recent studies have implicated ER resident proteins in the execution of PHP (Genç et al., 2017) or in baseline neurotransmission and synapse growth (Kikuma et al., 2017) at the Drosophila NMJ.
evidence: This statement references recent work on ER proteins and PHP.

claim: Both acute and chronic forms of PHP begin as instructive retrograde signals after perturbations are detected in the muscle.
source: Both acute and chronic forms of PHP begin as instructive retrograde signals after perturbations are detected in the muscle (Hauswirth et al., 2018; Orr et al., 2017a).
evidence: This statement references recent work on the initiation of PHP.

claim: Both acute and chronic forms of PHP involve a decrease in phosphorylation of muscle CaMKII levels, and converge upon the same signaling components in the presynaptic neuron.
source: These forms of PHP involve a decrease in phosphorylation of muscle CaMKII levels, and converge upon the same signaling components in the presynaptic neuron (Goel et al., 2017; Li et al., 2018; Newman et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement references recent work on the signaling mechanisms of PHP.

claim: Tor signaling converges on the same molecular targets as acute forms of PHP.
source: These studies suggest that Tor signaling converges on the same molecular targets as acute forms of PHP (Goel et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement references recent work on Tor signaling and PHP.

claim: The expression of any form of PHP (acute or chronic) appears to correlate with an increased intensity of active zone protein levels, such as CaV2/Cacophony, UNC-13, and the Drosophila CAST/ELKS homolog Bruchpilot.
source: First, the expression of any form of PHP (acute or chronic) appears to correlate with an increased intensity of active zone protein levels, such as CaV2/Cacophony (Gratz et al., 2019), UNC-13 (Böhme et al., 2019), and the Drosophila CAST/ELKS homolog Bruchpilot (Böhme et al., 2019; Goel et al., 2019a; Gratz et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement references recent work on active zone remodeling during PHP.

claim: The rapid induction of PHP does not require active zone protein increase in order to be functionally executed.
source: Unexpectedly, however, two of these studies also reported that the rapid induction of PHP does not require this protein increase in order to be functionally executed (Böhme et al., 2019; Goel et al., 2019a).
evidence: This statement references recent work showing that active zone remodeling is not required for acute PHP.

claim: Both RyR and IP3R have been shown to be critical for specific aspects of neuroplasticity and neurotransmission.
source: Both RyR and IP3R have been shown to be critical for specific aspects of neuroplasticity and neurotransmission (Berridge, 2016).
evidence: This statement references prior work on the roles of RyR and IP3R in neuroplasticity.

claim: Activities of both RyR and IP3R can activate molecules that drive plasticity, such as Calcineurin and CaMKII.
source: Activities of both RyR and IP3R can activate molecules that drive plasticity, such as Calcineurin (Victor et al., 1995) and CaMKII (Shakiryanova et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement references prior work on downstream effectors of RyR and IP3R.

claim: At rodent hippocampal synapses, electrophysiological measures like paired-pulse facilitation and frequency of spontaneous neurotransmitter release are modulated by RyR and/or IP3R function.
source: At rodent hippocampal synapses, electrophysiological measures like paired-pulse facilitation and frequency of spontaneous neurotransmitter release (Emptage et al., 2001) are modulated by RyR and/or IP3R function, as is facilitation of evoked neurotransmitter at the rat neocortex (Mathew and Hablitz, 2008).
evidence: This statement references prior work on the roles of RyR and IP3R in mammalian synapses.

claim: Activity of presynaptic voltage-gated calcium channels is modulated by intracellular calcium.
source: In addition to vesicle fusion apparatus, activity of presynaptic voltage-gated calcium channels is modulated by intracellular calcium (Catterall, 2011; Lee et al., 2000).
evidence: This statement references prior work on calcium channel modulation.

claim: Impairing factors needed for store-operated calcium release can mollify hyperexcitability phenotypes caused by gain-of-function CaV2 amino-acid substitutions.
source: Our own work at the NMJ has shown that impairing factors needed for store-operated calcium release can mollify hyperexcitability phenotypes caused by gain-of-function CaV2 amino-acid substitutions (Brusich et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement references the authors' own prior work on store-operated calcium release.

claim: Both pre- and postsynaptic voltage-gated calcium channels are critical for the expression of several forms of homeostatic synaptic plasticity.
source: Both pre- and postsynaptic voltage-gated calcium channels are critical for the expression of several forms of homeostatic synaptic plasticity (Frank, 2014b).
evidence: This statement references prior work on the role of calcium channels in homeostatic plasticity.

claim: In various neuronal populations, both RyR and IP3R interact with L-type calcium channels physically and functionally to reciprocally impact the opening of the other channel.
source: In various neuronal populations, both RyR and IP3R interact with L-type calcium channels physically and functionally to reciprocally impact the opening of the other channel (Chavis et al., 1996; Kim et al., 2007; Ouardouz et al., 2003).
evidence: This statement references prior work on interactions between store-operated and voltage-gated calcium channels.

claim: In presynaptic boutons, RyR calcium release follows action potential firing.
source: In presynaptic boutons, RyR calcium release follows action potential firing (Emptage et al., 2001).
evidence: This statement references prior work on the timing of RyR-mediated calcium release.

claim: Calcium imaging experiments show that both the acute expression and sustained maintenance of PHP requires an increase in presynaptic calcium following an action potential.
source: Calcium imaging experiments show that both the acute expression and sustained maintenance of PHP requires an increase in presynaptic calcium following an action potential (Müller and Davis, 2012).
evidence: This statement references prior work on calcium dynamics during PHP.

claim: Elevated IP3 levels in the case of chronically expressed PHP could allow IP3Rs and RyRs to open in a way that is time-locked with CaV2-mediated calcium influx or in a way to facilitate the results of later CaV2-mediated influx.
source: Because IP3Rs are activated by both free calcium and IP3, elevated IP3 levels in the case of chronically expressed PHP could allow IP3Rs and RyRs to open in a way that is time-locked with CaV2-mediated calcium influx or in a way to facilitate the results of later CaV2-mediated influx.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about how IP3 signaling might interact with calcium influx during PHP.
